newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Unocal keen to build Afghan peace pipelines.
newsitem.headline: Unocal keen to build Afghan peace pipelines.

text.p: Delivering gas and oil from Turkmenistan to Pakistan could promote peace in war-ravaged Afghanistan, the only route for the proposed pipelines, a Unocal Corp executive said on Tuesday.

"We believe the projects are an important part of the conflict resolution process," Marty Miller, the U.S. company's vice-president for new ventures, Middle East and Central Asia, told Reuters in an interview.

"They also have a strategic significance in the region in opening up Central Asia to world markets. The fundamentals are rock solid and when you look at the benefits you realise that sooner or later these pipelines are going to be built."
Asked how long Unocal would sustain its interest in view of the apparently intractable Afghan conflict, he said: "We are prepared to stay at a stage of readiness for quite some time."

Miller was visiting Pakistan, along with Unocal's executive vice-president Chris Taggart, to brief the caretaker government on the status of the projects and to lay to rest media reports that Unocal favoured the radical Islamic Taleban faction.
"We wanted to let the Pakistani government know that these reports are absolutely untrue and we remain absolutely neutral," Miller said.
Unocal had kept in touch with all Afghan factions and all of them had voiced support for the projects, he added.
Miller said Unocal supported United Nations efforts to broker a settlement between the Taleban and its rivals.
"Any final agreement (on the pipelines) would have to be with an entity that had broad internal support and a government with international recognition," he said.
No country has recognised the Taleban administration set up after the Islamic warriors swept into Kabul on September 27 and Afghanistan's seat at the United Nations is vacant.

Miller said Unocal, in partnership with Saudi Arabia's Delta Oil Company, had completed the project definition phase of the gas pipeline project and was ready for commercial talks. Work on the $2.5 billion oil project was not far behind.

The proposed gas pipeline would run 1,403 km (872 miles) from Turkmenistan's Dauletabad gas field to Pakistan, while the 1,677 km (1,015 miles) oil pipeline would run from Chardzou in Turkmenistan to a terminal on Pakistan's Arabian Sea coast.

Miller said the throughput of the $2 billion gas pipeline might be reduced to 12 billion cubic metres a year from 20 billion originally envisaged because Pakistan's projected natural gas demand was lower than first thought.
"We are also looking at a possible extension of the pipeline to India, which would open up an enormous market," he said.
Agreement between India and Pakistan on such an extension would ensure the pipeline would have a throughput of at least 20 billion cubic metres a year and reduce the cost of the gas.

Miller said no detailed pricing talks had taken place, but the gas was likely to be priced somewhere between Pakistan's target price of 90 percent of that of fuel oil equivalent and Turkmenistan's stated desire to sell its gas at $45 per thousand cubic metres at the Turkmen-Afghan border.
He said unnamed Japanese and Pakistani partners were likely to join the Unocal/Delta consortium in the first quarter of 1997.
The group already includes Turkmenrusgas, a joint venture between the Turkmen government and Russia's Gazprom company, with a five percent stake. Gazprom has its own 10 percent stake.
